patch.value: Release attribution is derived from a mutable timestamp while the immutable release stamp ships unused, so the changelog records what was touched instead of what shipped

The changelog generator resolves an item into a release window with closed_at ?? updated_at ?? created_at (pm-changelog generator.ts itemTimestamp). In this workspace 1,488 of 1,793 terminal items carry no closed_at, so 83 percent of shipped history is attributed by last-touch time. Any metadata write on those items — the exact writes the terminal relationship backfill, the close-reason backfill, and the duplicate-code rename all require — silently re-buckets decade-old work into the current release. The generator already supports a timestamp-independent alternative: a release window can declare a releaseTag and items whose release field matches are bucketed there regardless of timestamps. The release field is plumbed end to end (create --release, update --release, list --release, list --filter-release-missing) and zero of 2,068 items in this workspace carry a value. The tracker therefore relies entirely on a mutable field for a fact that is immutable once published.

The release cut stamps the release identifier onto every item it publishes, as an ordinary history-recorded mutation, so attribution is written once at the moment it becomes true; Historical release membership is backfilled deterministically from the tag containing each item's closing history entry, with an explicit residual list for items whose evidence is insufficient rather than a guessed value; Changelog generation prefers the stamped release identifier over any timestamp, and the check gate proves that editing metadata on an already-published item produces no changelog diff; A validation surface reports items that are terminal and unattributed, so the gap is measurable instead of invisible; The published changelog is byte-identical across the migration for every already-released window
Make release membership an immutable recorded fact rather than a side effect of the last edit

Every governance backfill this tracker still owes — terminal relationship lineage, close-reason evidence, duplicate-code repair — is gated not by its own risk but by the changelog re-bucketing the items it touches. Attribution by a stable key removes that coupling entirely.
Unblocks the terminal-history graph program and the resolution-evidence backfills, and makes release archaeology answerable from the tracker instead of from git tags
Release membership survives arbitrary later edits, and the changelog states what shipped in each release rather than what was most recently modified
The terminal graph backfill is the largest remaining structural deficit in the tracker, and this is the single constraint that makes it expensive

That field is plumbed end to end — create --release, update --release, list --release, list --filter-release-missing — and it is populated on 469 items, all of them terminal, with fourteen distinct values across which exactly one, v2026.3.12, matches one of the 76 real git tags. The rest are either a legacy taxonomy that predates date-based versioning (archive-2026q2 at 282 items, vnext at 144, v0.1 and variants at 34) or genuine release dates written without the v prefix the tags use (2026.5.14, 2026.6.10 and six more). Every active item carries no value at all. So the stable attribution key is not merely unused: it is populated with values that guarantee a miss, which reads as adopted while behaving as absent.

message: Correct the release-field measurement: 469 items do carry a value (all terminal, 14 distinct), but exactly one matches a real git tag; the earlier zero came from pm list --json omitting the field from its projection

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text: Measurement correction, 2026-07-26. An earlier reading of this workspace reported zero items carrying a release value. That was wrong, and the cause is worth recording because it will mislead the next measurement too: pm list --json omits non-projected fields, so release never appears in list output and a jq filter over it returns zero regardless of the stored data. Reading the .toon files directly gives 469 items with a release value, all of them terminal, across fourteen distinct values. Exactly one of those fourteen (v2026.3.12) matches one of the 76 git tags in this repository. Nine are release dates written without the v prefix the tags carry, and four are a legacy taxonomy (archive-2026q2, vnext, v0.1, v1-archive) that predates date-based versioning. No active item carries a value. The corrected picture strengthens the case rather than weakening it: the field is populated enough to look adopted and mismatched enough that releaseTag bucketing cannot use it, so a migration has to normalize existing values as well as stamp new ones.

value.text: Related read-surface trap worth fixing alongside this: pm list --json does not project the release field, so list --release filters correctly while the field itself is invisible in the output. Any migration script or audit written against list --json will measure zero and conclude the field is unused. pm list --filter-release-missing does work and reports all 275 active items as missing. The projection gap belongs to the list-projection family rather than to this item, but the migration must not be measured through it.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text: The mechanism is already shipped and merely unused: pm changelog generate accepts --respect-item-release, documented as treating an item release field as the authority. The generation script for this repository does not pass it, and could not usefully pass it today because only one of the fourteen stored values matches a tag. That makes the delivery order concrete — normalize and stamp the values first, then enable the flag in changelog:pm and changelog:pm:check, then prove the drag is gone by editing metadata on a published item and observing an unchanged changelog. No new generator capability is required.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
Acceptance criterion four is delivered, and the mechanism question this item raised is settled — with a correction to the assumption behind it.

The item states that the generator supports a timestamp-independent alternative via a release window declaring a releaseTag. It is stronger than that: under --all-release-tags, which is the mode this repository's changelog scripts already use, the item release field is unconditionally the attribution authority. The help text says so directly. No generator change and no script change were required. This was proved before any bulk write: stamping release v2026.6.30 onto closed pm-j1fj, a write that moved its updated_at to the present, produced a byte-identical CHANGELOG.md at 296,342 bytes.

Backfill executed and verified. Close instants derived from immutable history for all 1,795 terminal items: 1,683 from an op:close entry, 90 from an update that moved status into a terminal value, 22 from a create that was already terminal, zero fallbacks, zero unresolved. Control before writing: of the 307 items already carrying closed_at, the derived instant matched 307 and disagreed on 0. Mapping is the earliest tag whose creatordate is at or after the close instant, over 76 real tags. 1,782 stamped; the 13 that close after v2026.7.26 left unstamped, and they are exactly the current Unreleased membership. Post-write verification: 0 of 1,795 items disagree with the derivation.

Changelog consequence, reviewed: regeneration moved 295 items, every move matched the derivation, no items were added or removed, Unreleased stayed at 12, and changelog:pm:check returns check true. The 295 moves are corrections — those items were previously bucketed by a bulk updated_at touch rather than by when they shipped. Acceptance criterion seven asks for byte-identical output across the migration; that is the correct requirement for a mechanism change but not for a data correction, and the honest result is recorded here rather than claimed.

Remaining on this item: stamping at release-cut time so new closures are attributed automatically, the validation surface that reports terminal-and-unattributed items, the rejection of values that cannot match a tag, and the check gate proving a metadata write on a published item produces no diff. Without the first of those, attribution decays one release at a time. Delivery evidence lives on pm-3j6it6.
